Do not trade, give cash, hotel further, or end turn until light blues are armed."}}
message.reasoning:
I need to make a Monopoly decision.

I have $2314 and am on Ventnor Avenue. I control extensive monopolies with four houses on most properties. Several light blues, yellows, dark blues, and railroads are mortgaged.

I have two mortgaged utilities. The bank has 12 hotels and no houses left. Player 2 has $210 and cannot unmortgage any property. Players 3 and 4 are bankrupt. I will unmortgage the light blues and build four houses on each.

I will not trade or end my turn until the light blues are built. Player 2 cannot unmortgage any property, so the freed houses are safe. I am checking whether I actually freed twelve houses in the previous turn.

I ended my turn without freeing the twelve houses. The bank still has no houses left, so they remain locked on my properties.

I can only build hotels on the properties already at four houses. Building three hotels would return twelve houses to the bank. Hotel costs equal house costs, so I am checking the price for a brown hotel.

The prior plan to free twelve houses for two hundred dollars does not match the actual costs. Building three hotels on the pink group would cost three hundred dollars and return twelve houses. Selling four houses from a pink property would return only four houses for two hundred dollars.

I now see how to free twelve houses for two hundred dollars: build hotels on both brown properties and one pink or orange property. The light blue unmortgage costs total one hundred seventy-six dollars, and each light blue house costs fifty dollars.

The total cost for the light blue upgrade is nine hundred seventy-six dollars. I will begin this sequence now. Player two will roll next from Reading Railroad. A roll of two would hit my mortgaged Oriental Avenue, so I must unmortgage it before that roll.

Player two will roll from Reading Railroad. A roll of three lands on mortgaged Vermont. A roll of four lands on mortgaged Connecticut. Both pay no rent.

St. Charles Place, States Avenue, and Virginia Avenue each have four houses. Their rent is six hundred twenty-five dollars per house. A hotel brings seven hundred fifty dollars. These properties will kill player two's two hundred ten dollars.

Player two cannot survive any roll from Reading Railroad. Even Baltic Avenue at four houses costs four hundred fifty dollars, which exceeds player two's two hundred ten dollars. Every pink and orange property with four houses also kills him. Mediterranean Avenue at four houses costs two hundred fifty dollars, so it kills too. Player two survives only on unmortgaged properties that pay no rent, such as the mortgaged utilities and the Chance spaces.

Player two has a seventeen-in-thirty-six chance of surviving the next roll. He lands safely on Chance, Vermont, Connecticut, Electric Company, Pennsylvania Railroad, and Community Chest. He dies on St. Charles Place, States Avenue, Virginia Avenue, St. James Place, and Tennessee Avenue.

Three houses on each light blue is enough to kill player two. Oriental and Vermont at three houses cost two hundred seventy dollars. Connecticut at three houses costs three hundred dollars. Two houses would only cost ninety or one hundred dollars, which he could survive.

Player two could draw a Chance card and gain about one hundred fifty dollars, raising his cash to three hundred sixty dollars. Three houses would then cost two hundred seventy dollars, which he could survive, but four houses would cost four hundred or four hundred fifty dollars and kill him. I will build hotels on the light blues to free twelve houses for the bank. Selling houses is not an option because it would weaken my existing kill zones.

I had the rent figures wrong earlier. Mediterranean Avenue at four houses costs one hundred sixty dollars, which player two can survive with two hundred ten dollars. Baltic Avenue at four houses costs three hundred twenty dollars and kills him. Light blue properties with three or four houses still kill player two.

Player two has a fifty-three percent chance of dying on the next roll. A roll of five, seven, eight, ten, or twelve guarantees an instant kill. Rolls three, four, six, and nine let him survive. Three rolls out of thirty-six depend on Chance or Community Chest cards. Adding houses to the light blues would turn rolls three and four into guaranteed kills.

Unmortgaging the electric company is not worthwhile because a utility roll would cost at most forty-eight dollars. The plan to free houses by building hotels and then unmortgage the light blues is correct. I can only take one action this turn, so I am weighing whether to build three hotels for twelve houses or fewer.

Hotel costs are fifty dollars for brown properties and one hundred dollars for pink or orange properties. Building hotels on both browns plus one pink or orange property costs two hundred dollars and returns twelve houses. Hoteling Mediterranean Avenue would raise its rent from one hundred sixty dollars to two hundred fifty dollars, which would kill player two. Player two is currently on Reading Railroad, so this change only matters if he lands there later.

Standard Monopoly requires even building. A hotel counts as five houses, so building one hotel on a pink property while the others have four would violate the rule. I must either build hotels on all three pink properties or wait until they are evenly upgraded.

Even building allows a one-house difference, so a hotel on one pink property while the others have four is legal. I will not end my turn until the light blues are fully armed.

I will build three hotels in one action. I will upgrade Mediterranean Avenue and Baltic Avenue to hotels, and I will also upgrade one pink property. This frees twelve houses for the bank.

I will build the third hotel on St. Charles Place because it is the roll-five landing spot. Player two cannot build houses anyway, so keeping zero houses in the bank does not help block him.

Player two cannot unmortgage his red properties. The Kentucky, Indiana, and Illinois set costs roughly three hundred seventy-four dollars, which exceeds his two hundred ten dollars. He also lacks a complete green or yellow monopoly. Returning houses to the bank is therefore safe.

Unmortgaging the light blues first would leave them with zero houses, so player two could survive their doubled base rent. Either order works, but both steps are required before building.

I will build the three hotels first, then unmortgage the light blues in a separate action. I am weighing whether to spend two hundred dollars for twelve houses or only nine houses for three each.

Two hotels would free only eight houses, which is insufficient for three on each light blue. Even an even-build spread of three, three, and two would leave one property with just two houses, letting player two survive there. I must build three hotels to free twelve houses, or sell from the pink and orange properties.

I will build the three hotels now. Selling a house would weaken my kill zones, so that is not an option. I am preparing a short public message about upgrading the board. I am also checking unmortgage costs to plan the next steps.

Unmortgaging the light blues costs one hundred seventy-six dollars. Twelve houses cost six hundred dollars. After hotels, unmortgage, and houses, cash would be one thousand three hundred thirty-eight dollars. That is still plenty. Extra hotels on other properties are unnecessary because the twelve houses already freed are enough. The engine shows zero houses remaining in the bank.

Building three hotels in one action is safe because the engine returns houses to the bank rather than requiring them. I will not mortgage any properties or offer trades.
